draft.title: Time dilation
card: Time dilation is the effect that a clock moving relative to an observer is measured by that observer to run slow. The moving clock's own time between two events is called the proper time, t₀.
The observer's time is t = γt₀, where γ = 1 ÷ √(1 − v²/c²) is the Lorentz factor. The factor γ is always 1 or more, so t is longer than t₀.
At everyday speeds v is tiny next to c, so γ is almost exactly 1 and the effect cannot be noticed. It becomes large only when v is close to c.

Muons are made high in the atmosphere and last only about 2.2 microseconds in their own frame. Without dilation, most would decay before reaching the ground. Many are detected at ground level, which supports time dilation.
draft.remember: A moving clock is measured to run slow by the factor γ, and the effect is large only near the speed of light.

a.q: A spacecraft passes Earth at a speed where γ = 2. A clock on the spacecraft ticks off 3.0 s. How long does an Earth observer measure for this?
a.why: The 3.0 s is the proper time, measured on the moving clock. The Earth observer measures t = γt₀ = 2 × 3.0 = 6.0 s. Dividing by γ gives 1.5 s, but that reverses the effect: the moving clock runs slow, so the observer's time is longer.
a.clue: The moving clock's reading is the proper time, t₀.

b.q: Muons made high in the atmosphere reach the ground in far greater numbers than their 2.2 microsecond lifetime would allow. Which explanation fits special relativity?
opts: Ground observers measure a lifetime longer than 2.2 µs
Their lifetime in their own frame is longer than 2.2 µs
The muons travel faster than the speed of light
The distance to the ground is longer for the muons
b.why: The 2.2 µs is the lifetime in the muon's own frame. Ground observers measure the moving muon's clock running slow, so its lifetime is longer, by γ, and more muons arrive. The muon's own lifetime does not change, and nothing with mass can exceed c.
b.clue: Whose clock gives the 2.2 µs, and who measures the longer time?

b.best: Ground observers measure a lifetime longer than 2.2 µs
